Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, I declare open the fifth meeting of the 58th session of the Human Rights Council. Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, we will now proceed with the high-level segment. I have the honor of giving the floor to His Excellency Mr. Mihai Popsoi, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Moldova.

Excellency, you have the floor.

President, High Commissioner, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, this session of Human Rights Council is taking place in a rapidly evolving international context. While we continue to face appalling conflicts in Sudan and recent military hostilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo, we also see positive signs in other regions. We sincerely hope that the negotiated ceasefire in Gaza will hold, leading to sustainable peace based on a long-term two-state solution. Dear colleagues, these days we also mark three years since Russia unleashed its unprovoked, unjust war of aggression against Ukraine. This war, conducted by a nuclear power and a permanent member of the UN Security Council, has already caused destruction and suffering which will take generations to repair. Moldova stands in solidarity with Ukraine to resist the Russian aggression. My country continues to provide support to Ukrainian people, hosting more than 135,000 refugees, mostly women and children, providing humanitarian aid, helping with the transit of goods. As many as 70,000 Ukrainians are registered under temporary protection mechanism established in Moldova two years ago, benefiting from access to healthcare services, employment, education, including in their mother tongue. As discussions on peace are starting strongly, we believe that sustainable and comprehensive solution to this conflict entails the UN Security Charter being paramount, that it should bring Justice through robust accountability mechanisms for war crimes. Prevent any new war through robust security guarantees. And open the way for the reconstruction of Ukraine. No discussion on Ukraine without Ukraine. Mr. President, as a candidate country on its EU accession path, the Republic of Moldova is strengthening the rule of law, fighting against corruption, and promoting respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms. In line with our international commitments and policy objectives, we will spare no effort to ensure the implementation of human rights standards. Equally, as a candidate country for the seat in the Human Rights Council for 2027-29, Moldova will promote human rights as a foundation of a fair and just world, regardless of geographical area. Mr. President, the Republic of Moldova regularly updates the Council on human rights situation in the breakaway, transitional region of my country. This year, there is no exception. The situation continues to be dire, as the freedom of expression, of assembly, and of the press are still suppressed. Any dissenting voice or any show of opposition by local activists may result in a prison term on extremist charges, and we continue to receive notification in this regard. Criminal liability still stands for those who are daring to seek justice in international courts, such as the European Court of Human Rights. We welcome the recent release of a number of persons held behind bars in the Transnistrian region on political grounds. We call on the release of the remaining ones and hope this practice will not be repeated again. Let me also refer to the situation in the eight Latin script schools located in the region, which have been subject to constant and various forms of pressure and intimidation throughout the years. We urge the Russian Federation abide by international obligations and execute without further delay the European Court of Human Rights judgment in cases originating from the Transdniestrian region of Moldova and pay the just satisfactions awarded by the Court. As the Republic of Moldova takes over the presidency of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe between November 25 and May 26, the execution of judgments will be one of our priorities. We will also pay special attention to the fight against discrimination disinformation, propaganda, strengthening local democracy, the protection of children and women's rights. Mr. President, Moldova will stay engaged in common efforts for ensuring the Council remains effective. We adhere also to the calls for strengthening the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights by ensuring sustainable, predictable, and adequate funding. In the year of the 80th anniversary of the foundation of the UN, the role of the Office of the Human Rights Council remains pivotal. Thank you.
Thank you, Excellency. I now give the floor to His Excellency Archbishop Paul Gallagher, Secretary for Relations with States of the Holy See. Excellency, you have the floor.

Mr. President, this year, as the world grapples with the tragedy of numerous conflicts, global crises, and ongoing violations of human rights, Pope Francis has declared a Jubilee Year of Hope to be celebrated by the Catholic Church. It is the desire of the Holy See that the Human Rights Council will respond holistically and constructively to humanity's need for tangible signs of hope in the times we live in. Mr. President, the right to life is enshrined in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and is a prerequisite for the enjoyment of all other human rights. As Pope Francis affirms, All life must be protected at every moment, from conception to natural death, because no child is a mistake or guilty of existing, just as no elderly or sick person may be deprived of hope and discarded. Furthermore, the Holy See reiterates its call for the universal abolition of the death penalty. The demographic crisis calls for a renewed appreciation of the gift of life, motherhood, and of the family. The Holy See hopes that the 30th anniversary of the Beijing Conference will be an occasion to celebrate the many gifts that women uniquely possess and to recognize and support the vocation of motherhood. Human rights are universal and apply to all. including the estimated 125 million people forcibly displaced. Pope Francis has stated that these people cannot be treated like objects to be moved about. They have dignity and resources that they can offer to others. It is only by viewing things in this perspective that progress can be made in confronting a phenomenon that requires the contribution of all countries, not least through the creation of safe, regular pathways. It is worrying that almost half of the world's population lives in countries that spend more on debt repayment than on health or education. Therefore, I reiterate the call of Pope Francis to the international community to work towards forgiving financial debt as a matter of justice, not merely as a question of generosity. Moreover, there is also a need to recognize and address the ecological debt that exists between the global north and the global south. Furthermore, attempts to restrict religious freedom are an obstacle to lasting peace and integral development. Yet, across the world, around 380 million Christians continue to suffer high levels of persecution and discrimination for their faith. This Council can play a crucial role in combating discrimination against Christians, Jews, Muslims and members of other religions, and in ensuring religious freedom. Mr. President, The world is facing pressing issues which require a strong multilateralism that respects the equal sovereignty of States uses a common language and does not seek to manipulate multilateral documents by changing the meaning of terms or unilaterally reinterpreting the content of human rights treaties in order to advance divisive ideologies that trample on the values and beliefs of peoples. This is a form of ideological colonisation. that fractures relations between states and compromises the integrity of multilateral institutions, while diverting precious time, energy, and attention away from the issues that really matter. In a world in need of tangible signs of hope, the diplomacy of hope called for by Pope Francis could help this Council play a key role in healing the wounds of humanity and in giving multilateralism the new vitality it needs to address the complexities of our times. Thank you, Mr. President.

I thank His Excellency. Now I have the honor to give the floor to Her Excellency Ms. Maria Gabriela Sommerfeldt Rozero, Minister of Foreign Affairs and Human Mobility of Ecuador. Her Excellency, you have the floor by video.

Ecuador remains committed to defending, promoting, and protecting human rights, both in the universal and regional systems. My country has defended strengthening multilateralism and the principles of international cooperation and solidarity, which will foster the promotion and protection of human rights around the world. Ecuador, my country, was the first state in the world to have ratified the 27 legally binding international instruments in the area of human rights and has brought its law and practice into line with these principles. Since 2003, Ecuador has had a standing invitation to all United Nations special procedures mandate holders to visit the country, and we strive to ensure that commitments with the UN human rights treaty bodies and universal periodic review are met. Nevertheless, Ecuador and the whole region face a serious crisis of violence. This is the result of the activities of transnational organized crime groups, which attack citizens' security, state sovereignty and peaceful coexistence. I'm referring in particular to the alarming increase in the activity of criminal organisations that crosses borders. These unlawful networks have become a cancer which corrodes the social fabric of our countries and fuels corruption and violence. In this regard, we have proposed a number of visionary ideas to curb these groups which undermine peaceful coexistence between nations. When we held the presidency of the Security Council in December of 2023, Ecuador reiterated its commitment to building a fairer, more supportive and inclusive world. We believe that all countries, regardless of their size or power, have a role to play in promoting international peace and security. This holistic vision of peace and security has to be the beacon to guide our actions. We cannot allow transnational crime to continue to prosper at the expense of our nation's stability and wellbeing. We firmly believe that peace and security are factors for development. Thus, if we eradicate violence and combat transnational organized crime, then we will be achieving the goals which the Government of Ecuador has set itself. But we need to have international cooperation to this end. We shall continue to play a constructive role in the Human Rights Council and lead on a number of different resolutions and initiatives. We're also running to be a member of the Human Rights Council for the 2027-2029 mandate. In the past, the United Nations General Assembly has chosen us on three different occasions to join the Human Rights Council as a member, and a number of Ecuadorian experts have held high positions in the various mechanisms that are part of the universal inter-American human rights systems. It's against this backdrop that Ecuador will continue to adopt the necessary measures to promote human rights, empower women and girls, prevent and eradicate discrimination and violence, and to promote gender equality. We will continue to forge public policies and programs for the effective enjoyment of rights by children, adolescents, indigenous peoples, Ecuadorians of African descent, older persons, persons with disabilities, and others who are vulnerable. This is in line with international conventions to which Ecuador is a state party, and in line with our domestic law. Furthermore, my country is playing an active role in implementing the Global Compact for Refugees and for a safe, orderly, and regular migration. and we use a cross-cutting human rights-based approach for this. We have also amended our organic law on human mobility in order to strengthen the effective application of the constitutional mandate of equality and non-discrimination. This has been done by including a framework for preventing and protecting victims of human trafficking and migrant smuggling. We will continue to advocate that the international community pay the appropriate attention to the link between human rights and the environment. In this regard, my country has undertaken a number of different actions in order to tackle climate change, because we believe that climate change poses a threat to the enjoyment of human rights. Allow me to conclude by reiterating that Ecuador will continue to work on outstanding challenges and on the initiatives to improve legal frameworks and to strengthen institutional capacity using a human rights based approach and gender, disability and age perspectives. We will work in strict compliance with the principles of equality and non-discrimination with the aim of preserving and strengthening peace, security and development in Ecuador. We believe that cooperation among all stakeholders and solidarity are vital tools for preventing human rights violations. Thank you very much.
Thank you, Excellency. Now I have the honor to give the floor to Mr. Georg Danilov Georgiev, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Bulgaria. Excellency, you have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. Allow me to extend my warmest congratulations to His Excellency the Ambassador, Jorg Lauber, of Switzerland. on the occasion of his election as President of the Human Rights Council for 2025 and to express our full support for his efforts to advance dialogue, cooperation, and the use of digital technologies. I wish him and the Bureau of the Human Rights Council every success in their work. I would like to underline how important it is to ensure the independence, integrity, and sustainability of the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, as well as of the Office of Human Rights Council mechanisms and the UN treaty bodies. Bulgaria remains steadfast in its support for their efforts to uphold and promote human rights. Mr. President, just yesterday, the world marked three years since the Russian Federation launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. We reiterate our strongest condemnation of all violations of international human rights law and international humanitarian law committed in the course of Russia's aggression. Those violations demand full accountability. In this regard, we welcome the Human Rights Council's continued engagement on the human rights situation in Ukraine, which will stay high on our agenda during this session as well. We fully support the resolution extending the mandate of the Independent International Commission of Inquiry, which will be presented by Ukraine. In January, we commemorated the 80th anniversary of the liberation of Auschwitz. which solemnly reminded to us all about the need to combat intolerance, discrimination and hate, and to prevent war crimes and crimes against humanity. Ensuring accountability for the serious human rights violations and breaches of international humanitarian law is crucial for the prevention of future crimes and atrocities. Bulgaria remains firmly committed to combating impunity and promoting international criminal justice. We emphasize the important role of the International Criminal Court to end impunity, uphold the rule of law, and guarantee respect for the international law and human rights. Mr. President, in these turbulent times, marked by devastating conflicts, rising inquiries, and powerful emerging technologies, the international rules-based order with human rights at its core remains vital for the security, stability, and prosperity of the humankind. The promotion, protection and fulfilment of human rights are a fundamental prerequisite of the achievement of freedom, dignity, equality, democracy, rule of law, peace and sustainable development. These values and principles are at the heart of Bulgaria's foreign policy priorities. As a member of the Human Rights Council, our country underscores the central role of this body within the UN system. At a time when multilateralism is under increasing pressure and the Council's functioning faces new challenges, we believe it is imperative to offer a collective response. The upcoming 2026 review of the Human Rights Council's status presents an excellent opportunity to reaffirm the Council's mandate, highlight its pivotal role in the international system, and demonstrate the enduring value of multilateralism. Bulgaria will continue to support the efforts to promote the culture of peace, tolerance, and understanding. We regard as indispensable the role of the Human Rights Council for the achievement of human rights-based sustainable development goals. Bulgaria allocates equal attention to the needs, ensure adequate reactions of the Council to gross violations and abuses of human rights, and to exercise the Council's prevention functions. We seek to contribute to all endeavors to combat disinformation while strengthening media freedom and ensuring the safety of journalists. This year, we celebrate the 30th anniversary of the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action, a landmark achievement in the advancement of women's rights and equality between women and men. We firmly believe that concrete policies aimed to empower women and girls are crucial in order to foster sustainable development, social justice, and prosperity for all. In its national policies, Bulgaria continues to place a strong emphasis on the equality between women and men, as well as on the empowerment of women and girls. A visible testament to Bulgaria's commitment to this cause is the active participation of women in leadership roles across all sectors of society. Bulgaria remains dedicated to the advancement of the right to education for all children, motivated by the significant long-term benefits of early and pre-primary education for the cognitive and social development of children. We encourage all Member States to engage constructively in the governmental working group exploring the possibility of an optional protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child, which aims to consolidate the access to free education. Bulgaria is fully committed to the promotion of the rights of persons with disabilities and continuously encourage and facilitate their integration in all spheres of public life. It is important also to address the impact of the artificial intelligence on human rights, especially with regard to children's rights, the media freedom and the fight against disinformation. In conclusion, I would like to highlight again the leadership of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and his dedicated staff in the tireless strive to advance the cause of human rights around the world at this precious time. Let me also reaffirm Bulgaria's unwavering commitment to the principles of international law, universal human rights, dialogue, and continued strengthening of multilateral cooperation. These are the foundations for the progress that humankind has achieved so far, and they will continue to be the basis on which we can build a more just, inclusive, prosperous, and sustainable future for all of us. Thank you for the kind attention.
I thank the Foreign Minister of Bulgaria for his statement. And now I give the floor to Mr. Jan Lipavsky, Minister for Foreign Affairs of Czechia, by video.

Mr. Secretary General, High Commissioner Turk, President Lauber, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, We are living in difficult times. Armed conflicts, coups, and humanitarian crises are increasing. Human rights are under threat. It's our shared duty to defend them. This year, the United Nations mark its 80th anniversary. This is a moment to reflect on its founding principles. Tshisekela is a strong supporter of the UN human rights system. We are proud to serve on the Human Rights Council for the fifth time. The Council plays a key role in addressing the human rights crisis. We will not stand aside. Protecting human rights requires a united effort. Governments, civil society, activists, journalists, and media workers all have a role to play. If we fail, the consequences will be more suffering, greater inequality, and increasing instability. Women and girls must have full protection online and offline. The 30th anniversary of the Beijing Action Platform remind us of the power of inclusion. Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine continues to cause enormous human suffering. We must defend international law, condemn attacks on civilians, and hold Russia accountable for its crimes. Russia's occupation of Crimea and parts of Donbas has led to severe repressions. People face persecution and economic hardship. We call on Russia to release all political prisoners, including Iryna Dalinovich and Emir Hussein Kuku. Czechia stands with Ukraine. We support its people at home and abroad. Our help is diplomatic, political, financial, material. Sanctions must continue. In Russia, human rights are also under attack. The Kremlin silences critics and crushes freedoms. People face unfair trials, long prison sentences, and harsh reprisals. Russia must stop oppressing its own citizens and release all political prisoners. Human rights violation persists in many parts of the world. In Iran, Afghanistan, North Korea, Myanmar, Belarus, China, and other countries, people suffer daily. The world cannot look away. In Georgia, the right to peaceful assembly is under threat. Czechia will again present a resolution on this June. Our own history shows why these freedoms must be protected. Digital rights matters. The Human Rights Council must help shape global standards. We support stronger cooperation between human rights experts and technology specialists. Mr. President, Czechia will work with its partners to strengthen this Council and uphold human rights worldwide. I thank you.

Mr. Vice President, Excellencies, At the elections held a few months ago, the people of Sri Lanka elected a new government with a strong mandate to direct the country towards economic, social, and political transformation. The results of these elections reflected a unified voice from people of all regions of the country, ethnicities, and religions. The current Parliament is the most inclusive in our history, with a record number of women, including two from the Malay community and a visually impaired person. This inclusivity represents Sri Lanka's new path, focused on upholding the rights of all its people irrespective of gender, ethnicity or other grounds. The economic crisis affected all segments of the population, especially the poorest and the most vulnerable. Having stabilised the economy, the Government is currently in the process of laying the foundation toward economic transformation and greater economic democratisation through fair distribution of opportunities. We are acutely aware of the continuing impact of the economic challenges on our people, particularly the most vulnerable, and decisive steps are being taken to advance their economic and social rights. In the national budget for 2025, we have committed to a series of measures to extend much-needed relief to the people, including increased allocation for social welfare and security. Special attention has been paid to improving the socio-economic conditions and address critical needs such as resettlement, housing, compensation and infrastructure development in the northern and eastern provinces. Through the Clean Sri Lanka project launched by the President on 1st January, the government has introduced a new political culture and commitment to moral and ethical governance. The Government will prioritise integrity and addressing issues of mismanagement and corruption. The fundamental and long-standing principles of democracy and freedom enshrined in our Constitution will be respected and safeguarded while protecting the human rights of all citizens. Administrative, political and electoral processes will be activated towards this end. The Government has pledged to take tangible steps to further advance national unity and reconciliation. The President has proposed to declare a Sri Lankan Day, in line with our vision for a reconciled Sri Lanka and bridging gaps between communities. We will ensure that the domestic processes established to address remaining challenges from the conflict will continue their work in an independent and credible manner. Domestic institutions such as the Office on Missing Persons, Office for Reparations and Office for National Unity and Reconciliation will be strengthened. The contours of a truth and reconciliation framework will be further discussed with a broad cross-section of stakeholders to ensure a process that has the confidence of all Sri Lankans. Our aim is to make the domestic mechanisms credible and sound within the constitutional framework. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission will be empowered to investigate acts of violence that give rise to tensions within Sri Lankan society. The Government is fully cognisant of the responsibility that accompanies the people's mandate to fulfil the aspirations for a just, fair and prosperous society. As we work towards national unity, reconciliation and inclusive development, the continued encouragement and support of the international community will be important. Sri Lanka is an active member of the UN and a party to all core human rights instruments. We regularly engage with treaty bodies and special procedures. In the past few years, We have received visits from over 10 special procedures and engaged productively with treaty bodies, most recently with the CEDAW Committee, ICCPR and the UPR. We are committed to genuine dialogue and cooperation on human rights through continuous and constructive engagement. Sri Lanka stands ready to support this Council in addressing the pressing global challenges in a balanced and holistic manner, in line with its founding principles of universality, impartiality, objectivity and non-selectivity. We believe that States must be encouraged and empowered to address their challenges through robust national human rights frameworks, supplemented by assistance upon request. We will continue to work in a constructive spirit of dialogue and cooperation with the UN and this Council within our national legal framework. Thank you very much.

I would like to thank His Excellency the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Sri Lanka.

Minister for Foreign Affairs of Denmark, Mr.

President, dear colleagues, it is an honor to address the Council. As we all know, human rights are crucial to human dignity, quality, freedom, peace, and sustainable development. These principles form the very foundation of a good life. Unfortunately, that is far from the reality for many people around the world. Let me provide just a few examples. Three years ago, Russia launched its illegal, unprovoked and unjustified full scale invasion of Ukraine. Civilians have been forced to flee their homes. Civilians have been traumatized. Civilians have been killed. We must all continue to stand by the Ukrainian people for as long as necessary. In Gaza. The humanitarian situation remains catastrophic following Hamas's horrific terror attack on 7 October 2023. Far too many civilians have been killed. The events that have unfolded over the last 16 months clearly illustrate the need for a long-term solution to the decades-long conflict. We have seen some positive momentum during the past month. But we must continue to focus on taking steps towards sustainable peace. A two-state solution is the only viable long-term solution. In the Eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, the current escalation of the conflict is deeply concerning, as also discussed by the Council in the special session a few weeks ago. Reports of sexual and gender-based violence, including cases of mass rape, are horrific. The people of the DRC deserve peace. The people of the Great Lakes region deserve peace. International borders must be respected. There is no military solution to the conflict, only a political one. In Myanmar, the junta continues its brutal crackdown, oppressing its people. Our voice in support of the people of Myanmar is therefore still important. And unfortunately, I could continue this list. The United Nations play a vital role in maintaining peace and security and in ensuring a stable and just global order. The UN is the only place where the whole world can come together to advance peace, security and fundamental freedoms for all. The importance of international law cannot be overstated. No nation can stand alone. Global challenges demand global solutions. We cannot afford to move backward. Our collective goal must be in a world free of war, a world free of poverty, a world free from the suppression of human rights. Thank you.

I thank the Foreign Minister of Denmark for his statement.

I would like to give the floor to His Excellency, Mr. Paul-Marie Gouanjou, Minister of Justice and Garde des Sceaux of Gabon. You have the floor, Your Excellency.

Excellency, President of the Human Rights Council, Ministers, Ambassadors, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, please allow me at the outset to convey the greetings of the Government of the Transition and the Gabonese people to the international community and all the different states and institutions present. I would also like to pay tribute to the Human Rights Council and all its mechanisms for their work to promote human rights. I would also like to congratulate Ambassador Jorg Lauer, the Swiss Permanent Representative, for having been elected to the presidency of the Council for 2025. I would also like to congratulate his predecessor, Omar Znaiber, Ambassador and Permanent Representative of Morocco for the excellent presidency last year. And last, I would like to convey my highest esteem to Mr. Volker Turk, High Commissioner for Human Rights, and his team for their tireless efforts to promote and protect human rights, despite the challenges they face. President. I'm honored to represent his Excellency Brigadier General Brice Clotaire Oligui N'Gema, President of the Transition, President of the Republic and Head of State, and I do so by reiterating Gabon's commitment to multilateralism and the principles of human rights. But these principles are being buffeted by a plethora of crises this year. But from our point of view, our response has to be by strengthening multilateral institutions and by making human rights a cornerstone of our societies. I would also like to inform you of the main developments that have occurred in Gabon since the 55th session following the coup of liberation in August 2023. The transitional authorities determined to respect human rights, and over the past six months, this has been reflected in consistent efforts and actions at national and international level with support from our partners. When it comes to co-operating with human rights mechanisms, I am pleased to inform you that my country has received the visit of the Sub-Committee on the Prevention of Torture in March of last year, and we have also submitted our periodic reports to the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment and the Convention for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination. On a national front, a number of measures have been taken with our partners to ensure effective enjoyment of human rights. Last January, we organized a workshop for the members of the national mechanism for drafting reports on using databases and adoption of the national action plan for implementing the recommendations from the fourth UPR cycle. We enacted Act 023 of 2024 last November to reorganize the National Human Rights Commission. This is a watershed for achieving human rights in Gabon. On the 12th of February of this year, we also published a call for candidates, and the new members will be selected over the coming months by the National Assembly. We also enacted Decree 0133 on 27 March last year, which establishes, organises and regulates the functioning of the National Preventive Mechanism on Human Trafficking. This is a coordinating body which will deal with human trafficking and will strengthen the existing legal arsenal on this subject. When it comes to criminal justice, we have amended the Criminal Code and the Criminal Procedure Code to include offences and reparation for violations of human rights in order to ensure better protection of these rights. And when it comes to health, I'm pleased to mention that the government has gradually taken action to implement strategic projects which will improve healthcare, strengthen governance of healthcare, and ensure universal access. President, since August 2023, the transitional authorities have been committed to a road map which sets out political and institutional reform which will enable us to return to peaceful and safe constitutional order prior to holding elections. These reforms have involved all stakeholders in our country and have focused above all on the holding of a national inclusive dialogue from the 2nd to the 30th of April last year, with over 680 participants, including participants from the diaspora. And we also adopted a new constitution following a referendum. It enshrines, amongst other things, a seven-year presidential mandate, which can be renewed once. And there will be no prime minister. And one specific feature is that power cannot be handed on from one member of a family to another. We also strengthened the rule of law and the grounds for national reconciliation and social cohesion. We also adopted Organic Law 001 of the 19th of January of this year, establishing the electoral code, which brings in a number of novelties which will simplify the legal framework and ensure the transparency and calendar for elections. Prisoners will be allowed to vote, and there will be quotas for women and youth, 30 per cent and 20 per cent respectively. Involving women in the electoral process is part and parcel of our resolve to implement the Beijing declaration and programme of action 30 years after its adoption. When it comes to that, we will spare no effort to strengthen the rights of women, promote gender equality and combat violence against women by adapting a national strategy for gender equality. President, ladies and gentlemen, we're holding a session today as Gabon moves into a new republic based on a new constitution, strengthening the rule of law, freedoms and democratic governance. In fact, my country is moving towards the end of the transitional period. which will be marked by the holding of presidential elections on 12 April, to be followed by local elections. I would like to take this opportunity to sincerely thank all our bilateral, regional and multilateral partners for supporting us in stabilising our country and returning to a safe and peaceful constitutional order. My sincere thanks to you, Minister. Minister of Justice from Gabon.

His Excellency, Mr. Andreas Kravik, State Secretary of Foreign Affairs of Norway, Excellency Eide Flø.

Excellencies, Mr. President, Over the past year, the world has again witnessed an unacceptable number of violations of human rights and international humanitarian law. The UN Charter, international humanitarian law, and human rights must be respected and protected. Violations are unacceptable. If states can safely violate international law, its credibility collapses. And, obviously, it will be harder to uphold international law in the future. Yesterday, in the UN headquarters in New York, the vast majority of UN member states gathered around defending international law, the UN Charter, and a sustainable peace for Ukraine. In Palestine, in Ukraine, in Sudan, and in other conflicts and crises, human rights defenders continue to be essential in promoting and protecting all human rights for everyone. We invite all States and civil society to engage in constructive and transparent negotiations, and hope that the resolution will enjoy the Council's consensual support. Finally, we look forward to working with all of you to uphold our shared commitment to the core values of the UN Human Rights Council. I thank you for your attention.

Mr. President, as a candidate country for the HRC 2028-2030, Greece reiterates its unwavering readiness to contribute substantially to the long-term effectiveness of the United Nations system. Together, we can build a world where human dignity is not just an aspiration, but a reality for all future generations. Thank you.
I thank Your Excellency for your statement. Now, I give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Nuno Sampaio, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs and Cooperation of Portugal, Excellency Efraim.

President, Excellencies, I'd like to thank the Secretariat for having enabled me to speak Portuguese. We defend an effective international protection system which prevents human rights violations and abuse and which ensures that perpetrators are held to account. an independent system which safeguards the independence of the High Commissioner and his office, which continues to strengthen treaty bodies and the Council's various mechanisms, and which allows all stakeholders to take part, namely small island developing states and the least developed countries. the trust fund for whom Portugal has made a contribution to. Also in June, we'll present a resolution on the right to education and here in Geneva, we'll continue to lead the group of friends on national mechanisms for implementation, reporting and follow-up on international human rights obligations and recommendations. We will work along with Morocco and Paraguay to promote the international network of those mechanisms, and we hope to contribute to that process by holding the third international seminar in Lisbon. In a few days' time, we will have the adoption of the outcome of Portugal's universal periodic review. We believe this is a vital tool for constructive dialogue between States, and we will pursue our efforts, which we believe are in priority areas: the abolition of the death penalty, combating racism, protecting the human rights of young people and migrants. This year, is also a key year for promoting gender equality and women's rights. We're commemorating the 30th anniversary of the adoption of the Beijing Declaration and Platform of Action and the 25th anniversary of Security Council Resolution 1325 on women, peace and security. We eagerly await the outcome of the 69th session of the Commission on the Status of Women, in which we will actively participate. I would like to conclude, President, by reiterating Portugal's support for this Council. In keeping with our tradition of building bridges and the principles that we defend and the commitments that we take on, we shall promote constructive and inclusive dialogue, because we believe that Achieving human rights is always work in progress. And so we need everybody to take part in it. I would like to thank His Excellency Mr. Nandu Sampaio for his statement. And now I give the floor to Her Excellency Ms. Kang In-soon, Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Korea. Excellency, you have the floor.

Mr. Vice President, distinguished delegates, It is my second time addressing this august chamber following last year. And this year, I am standing before you with an even keener sense of responsibility as the Republic of Korea has embarked on its role as a member of the Human Rights Council. We celebrate the eighth anniversary of the UN and recall its spirit rooted in humanity's inherent longing for peace. Yet we still witness grave human rights situations unfolding in all corners of the globe. The war against Ukraine just reached its third year yesterday, and it has been further complicated by strengthened military ties between Russia and the DPRK. Daily, we hear reports of the eroding human rights situation in Gaza and the DRC. The rise of emerging technologies is adding to the complexities of human rights challenges like a Pandora's box. As rightly observed by the High Commissioner, the key to resolving today's conflicts and crises rest in greater respect for human rights, not less. In this regard, 2025 offers a fitting opportunity to double down on our efforts in enhancing human rights as we start to implement the Pact for the Future adopted last year. As a member of the Human Rights Council, we will constructively engage with the international community, focusing on the following key priorities. First, We reiterate our unwavering belief in the Council and UN human rights mechanisms as a bastion of promoting and protecting human rights. Human rights are universal, and every voice counts. The Council plays an indispensable role in helping developing countries build the capacity to advance human rights norms and policies. Korea will continue to support such endeavors to ensure that human rights-based approaches are effectively implemented around the world. Second, the digital transformation. It is reshaping our world, and it presents both opportunities and challenges for human rights. Recognizing these transformative developments, Korea has made it a priority to tackle these complexities through a human rights-based approach. We are committed to leveraging our digital expertise to help the Council navigate the evolving human rights landscape in the digital age. In this regard, we will table our fourth resolution on this critical issue at the 59th session. Third, we must do more to protect women, girls, and other vulnerable groups, especially in times of escalating conflicts and protracted crises. This year marks 30 years since the Beijing Declaration and 25 years since UN Security Council Resolution 1325. It is a crucial moment to renew our wholehearted commitment to gender equality. Korea has long supported the WPS agenda. And we have been promoting survivor-centered responses to gender-based violence in conflict. As a country with a historical experience of women and girls victimized as a comfort to women, we view the WPS agenda as a particularly relevant and significant. We will continue to work together with the Japanese government to restore the honor and dignity of the comfort women and to help to heal their psychological wounds. At the last June's Security Council briefing on the human rights situation in the DPRK, the High Commissioner accurately captured the dire situation on the ground, a stifling claustrophobic environment where life is a daily struggle devoid of hope. The DPRK's deployment of its troops to Russia once again highlights the linkage between the DPRK's human rights abuses and its ramifications for international peace and security like two sides of the same coin. Reportedly, DPRK soldiers are drawn to the battlefield unaware of their involvement in the real combat, and trained to commit suicide when captured, which is incompatible with the right to life. We are deeply concerned about the inhumane treatment of the DPRK escapees being forcibly repatriated, including extrajudicial executions, arbitrary detentions, and reinforced -- enforced disappearances, as reported by the multiple UN special procedures. We reiterate our call for the states to respect the principle of non-refoulement. My government once again strongly urges the DPRK to immediately resolve all issues relating to abductees, detainees, and unrepatriated prisoners of war, including the prompt release of the three Korean missionaries, Kim Jong-uk, Kim Gook-ki, and Choi Choon-gil. We strongly urge the DPRK to heed the international community's recommendations made during last year's UPR and take prompt actions to bring about fundamental change in its dire human rights situation. And we look forward to the release of the High Commissioner's comprehensive report, which updates the human rights situation in the DPRK since 2014. Rising from the ashes of war, my country overcame devastation, poverty, and national division. We have never relented in striving to build a nation founded on freedom, democracy, and prosperity. The journey was arduous, and it remains so. But time and again, we have proved our resilience. The road to promoting and protecting human rights is not straightforward. Korea, based on our experience and strong sense of resilience, will remain a dedicated partner in navigating this path. Thank.

You.

I thank Her Excellency. Madam, the Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Korea. I now give the floor to His Excellency, Mr. Neil Richmond, Minister of State for International Development and Diaspora of Ireland.

Excellency, you have the floor.

Mr. Vice-President, ladies and gentlemen, it is a privilege to address the Human Rights Council at the opening of its 58th session. It is 70 years since Ireland joined the United Nations. Then, like now, we did not take our role as a UN member state lightly, but made a firm commitment to the multilateral rule-based order and to the UN Charter. A few short months ago, all States here pledged a new beginning to multilateralism by signing the Pact for the Future and committing to human rights as an integral part of the UN system. As we convene for this new session of the Human Rights Council, we also restate our commitment to this Council, the primary UN human rights body. Our presence here this week is a show of unity in the face of division, of support to the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, to international law, and to upholding, promoting, and defending human rights. In times of crisis like we face today, it is difficult not to lean into division and distrust. However, it is also in these moments that we can and must stand secure in our commitment to the principles of interrelated, interdependent, and indivisible human rights. Today, like 70 years ago, I restate Ireland's commitment to a rules-based international order and to a constant, persevering dedication to peace. Mr. Vice-President, this week, three years ago, Russia made clear its disdain for the UN Charter and international human rights law. The Commission of Inquiry established by this Council has found that violations of human rights and international humanitarian law, as well as war crimes, have been committed in the context of Russia's brutal, illegal war of aggression against Ukraine. The international community must continue to condemn such actions and ensure that perpetrators of human rights violations and abuses are held to account. Ireland will continue to call for an end to Russia's war of aggression and violations of international law and for a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in Ukraine based on the UN Charter and with respect for Ukraine's territorial integrity and sovereignty. Last week marked 500 days since the brutal attacks perpetrated by Hamas and other terrorist organisations on Israel. Ireland unreservedly condemns these attacks and the taking of hostages. Last month, we welcomed the long-awaited ceasefire and hostage release agreement in Gaza. This brought much-needed hope and relief to the people of both Israel and Palestine. We need to see the ceasefire agreement fully implemented in all its phases, including the release of all hostages. There must also be continuing entry of humanitarian aid at scale, the provision of basic services, and a framework for the return of those displaced from their homes within Gaza. We must also remain focused on the deteriorating situation in the West Bank. Ultimately, Implementation of the two-state solution remains the only way to ensure lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike. In Sudan, the Sudanese armed forces and the rapid support forces and their allied movements and militias have shown utter disregard for human rights. They must comply with their obligations to protect civilians, humanitarian workers and human rights defenders from harm and allow rapid and unimpeded humanitarian relief to all areas under their control. In Yemen, attacks against civilians by all parties to the conflict should be independently investigated to ensure accountability and enhance the protection of Yemeni civilians. In Afghanistan, the High Commissioner has determined that systematic gender persecution is being perpetrated by the Taliban. The Taliban must revoke all discriminatory decrees and all other measures that seek to eradicate women and girls' access to education, work and public services and that restrict their freedom of movement. Ireland is firmly committed to protecting and advancing both civil and political and economic, social and cultural rights. In recent years, the Human Rights Council has addressed the human rights implications of climate change. We have discussed how to enhance global protection against business-related human rights abuses, advocated for a human rights-based approach to new and emerging technologies, promoted gender equality, and advanced guidance on the elimination of all forms of racial discrimination and the prevention of violence and discrimination against LGBTI+ persons. A crucial component of this process is the constant open engagement with civil society partners. We have and must continue to advance protections for civil society and for human rights defenders. This council must be enabled to fulfil its role as the primary intergovernmental body for the promotion and protection of human rights globally. The Office of the High Commissioner must be adequately resourced and empowered to carry out its vital work. The guidance and recommendations of special procedures and of the treaty body committees must be heeded. Respect for human rights is where our values and interests align. It is through more respect for human rights that we achieve peace, prosperity, and sustainable development. Mr. Vice-President, in conclusion, as you will be aware, Ireland is seeking membership of the Human Rights Council for the term 2027-2029. If elected, we will protect and champion the universality of human rights and the principle of non-discrimination. We will be an advocate for prevention and for accountability. And we will work in partnership and good faith with all who share our commitment to multilateralism and the values and principles set out in the UN Charter and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Guram Minalgv, and thank you very much.

I would like to thank you, His Excellency. And now I give the floor to Son Excellence, Madame Isabelle Beraud Amadei.

Ms. Isabelle Beraud Amadei, Councillor of Government and Minister of Foreign Relations and Cooperation of Monaco.

President of the Human Rights Council, High Commissioner, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, at the very outset, I would like to reaffirm once again the paramount importance for Monaco of respect for human rights, international law, and our common commitment to the purposes and principles of the United Nations. A few weeks ago, I had the honor of leading the Monaco delegation to the ceremonies organized as part of the 80th anniversary of the liberation of the Auschwitz-Birkenau concentration camp. These moving commemorations honored the memory of millions of victims of human barbarism and highlighted the justification of the struggle for human rights, their universality and indivisibility. This is a constant struggle and one that is more relevant than ever. While geopolitical tensions, regional conflicts, interstate conflicts, and humanitarian crises persist, It is our shared responsibility always to defend the values upon which the UN system was built. There is no place for war in it, nor for unacceptable living conditions into which a large portion of humanity have been plunged. Thus, in Ukraine, three years to the day since the start of the Russian aggression, the guns have still not been silenced. Grave human rights violations continue there, as confirmed by reports submitted to this Council by your Office, Mr. High Commissioner, and by the International Commission of Inquiry. This documentation work is invaluable and indispensable with a view to establishing responsibility. Once again this year, Monaco will support the renewal of the Commission's mandate. Regarding the situation in the Middle East, The Principality of Monaco welcomes the cessation of hostilities in the Gaza Strip and Lebanon and the release of hostages. The very heavy human and material toll is appalling. Monaco reaffirms that the solution to any crisis can only be political. The process of peace and reconstruction will be lengthy and costly. It can only be conducted properly in a climate of peace and security for the civilian populations of the region. and within the framework of the two-state solution, which we continue to call for and wish for. The witness testimony and evidence gathered by the Commission of Inquiry and the Mechanism on Syria will be valuable to establish responsibility and to combat impunity. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, Monaco reaffirms that peace, sustainable development and human rights are indivisible. This Council is therefore key to uphold our vision of a peaceful, just world where all can live in dignity. The commissions of inquiry and fact-finding missions mandated by the UN play an important role in responding to violations of international law and international humanitarian law. This is why, very recently, regarding the events in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, Monaco supported the establishment of a fact-finding mission during the extraordinary session held on 7 February. I could also have mentioned many other situations of particular concern, especially concerning the rights of women and minorities in many countries. In this context, I assure you, Mr. High Commissioner, that the Principality will maintain this year once again its political and financial support for your office. I wish the Council every success in its work and I assure you of the total commitment of the delegation of Monaco to this end. I thank you.

I thank Her Excellency Ms. Isabelle Pierrot-Amadei for the statement.

Her Excellency Ms. Melita Gabric, State Secretary for Multilateral Affairs, Economic Diplomacy and Development Cooperation of Slovenia. Excellency, you have the floor.

Mr. President, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, It is an honor to address this esteemed Council on behalf of the Republic of Slovenia, a country firmly committed to upholding the principles of dignity, equality, and justice for all. The UN was born out of the ashes of the Second World War. As we commemorate this anniversary, we also remember the liberation of Auschwitz-Birkenau and the horrors of the Holocaust. This year, we also commemorate the 30th anniversary of the Srebrenica genocide. These tragedies remind us of the consequences of hatred, intolerance, and the failure to protect the most vulnerable. They compel us to renew our pledge, never again. Yet today, we face some 70 conflicts around the world, causing immense suffering and destruction, from Ukraine, where it has been three years since the unprovoked and illegal Russian aggression, to Sudan, where millions are subject to violence, displacement, and hunger. While we see some steps in the right direction in the Middle East, there remains an urgent need to ensure that the fundamental human rights of all people, including of the people in Gaza, are respected and that they can live in dignity and safety. All this underscores the urgent need for collective action, as human rights are also the very foundation of peace and security. The UN Human Rights Council plays a central role in this endeavor. Slovenia strongly supports, from the very outset, the Council and the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights in their efforts to address violations, promote justice, and prevent future atrocities. Prevention must remain at the very core of our work, as only through early action can we avert the escalation of conflicts and protect human dignity. As the High Commissioner reminds us, human rights are a low-cost investment with high returns. As a member of the Security Council, Slovenia firmly believes that human rights must be an integral part of all the Security Council deliberations. For my country, the rights of those who are marginalized are a priority. On the 30th anniversary of the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action and the 25th anniversary of the UN Security Resolution 1325 on women, peace, and security, Slovenia reaffirms its commitment to gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls. In the face of rapid demographic change, the human rights of older persons should receive more attention. We believe it is time to take concrete action to address the existing gaps in human rights protection so that older persons can enjoy their human rights on an equal basis and participate actively in societies. Similarly, we must advance the implementation of the right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment, a right that Slovenia has been an avid promoter of. As we face manifold challenges. We must never lose sight of our responsibility to uphold the human rights of every individual. Together, we can and must make a difference. Thank you.

Thank you, Your Excellency, Ms. Melita Gebre for her statement. Now we give the floor to Her Excellency, Ms. Varsen Agabikian, Minister of State for Foreign Affairs of the State of Palestine. Excellency, you have the floor.

I thank His Excellency for his statement. Now I give the floor to Ms. Marjana Svorc-Lajic, President of the International Committee of the Red Cross.

Vice President, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, Today, violations that were once considered abhorrent have disturbingly become normalized in conflicts around the world. I stand before you to remind us of an undeniable truth. Every patient killed in a hospital bed, every family buried, under the rubble of their home, every hostage stolen from their loved ones and every prisoner tortured and deprived of basic dignity, every city levelled and every village destroyed. These are not unfortunate realities of war. They are a betrayal. We must not become numb to the fact or that fact. or we risk sleepwalking into a world where the barriers that once restrained brutality in war are removed. The scale of suffering we witness is not inevitable. It is the direct result of dismissive interpretations of international humanitarian law. But people have the power to change course. It will require, though, courage and leadership to move past political divisions and recommit to the fundamental belief that human life must transcend political divides, both in war and in peacetime. Excellencies, together, international humanitarian law and international human rights law share a common goal: to protect human life, health, and dignity, no matter what country you were born in or what side of the front line you live on. These bodies of law are mutually reinforcing. They need one another. The erosion of respect for one contributes to the erosion of the other. In war, how can the right to health be fulfilled if hospitals are bombed? How can the right to food prevent hunger if crops are destroyed? How can children see their right to education come true if schools are attacked? There is no right to life when civilians and the infrastructure that they rely on for survival are systematically targeted. International humanitarian law exists to protect them in times of war. The way wars are fought today will inform the way they are fought tomorrow. Where basic humanitarian rules are violated, rebuilding costs skyrocket and new security threats arise. We can choose a different path, one that promotes life, stability and prosperity. This starts with committing to international humanitarian law and making it a political priority. The ICRC, together with Brazil, China, France, Jordan, Kazakhstan, and South Africa, in September launched a global initiative to revive political commitment to international humanitarian law. Many states have since joined, and I hope that many more will continue to do so. Mr. Vice President, at this time of tectonic political shifts, the pressure for humanitarian organizations to pick a side is at a fever pitch. We, as the ICRC, will not bend to it. If we did, we would lose our ability to help people on all sides in the world's most contentious theatres of armed conflict. States do not need to be neutral, but they need the ICRC to fulfil the role. A neutral humanitarian body is a vital feature of the international peace architecture, and without which the entire system is weaker. It is by upholding our strict impartiality and confidentiality that we ensure our ability to stand for humanity. I thank you.

Europe.

This has been the case for exactly three years now. The Council of Europe has made Ukraine its top priority. We are committed to three major pillars of action. All three of them are rooted fundamentally in the defense of human rights. One of them is justice. with zero impunity for any violations of human rights that may have been perpetrated. Second, protection of Ukrainian children. And third, reconstruction of the country. The principle behind this is very clear, the principle for action, no to impunity. In recent weeks, we have seen significant progress in setting up a claims commission based on the register for damage. and the creation of a special tribunal for the crime of aggression. This is another priority. Now, I have just appointed a special envoy for the situation of children in Ukraine. Now, Vice President, Excellencies, I would like to give you the following argument. There can be no effective, stable protection of human rights without functioning rule of law. There can be no stable, rule of law that is accepted and that functions without democracy that functions. And there is no democracy without massive investment in education and without acceptance by everyone of the rules, without everyone abiding by the democratic rules of play. I am saying this because I believe that fundamentally, democracy is essential to ensure stable and effective defense of human rights. And everyone in the world, including in Europe, we see that safeguarding democracy is a daily struggle. This is one of the major works of progress that we have. We have the tools to counter democratic backsliding, the rise in authoritarianism and populism, disinformation, and everything that threatens our democratic societies. To defend human rights, we need some conditions. These conditions do not mean accepting that we live in a world that is dominated by power, by violence, by a balance of power and impunity. As the UN Secretary-General said in September in New York, the level of impunity around the world that we live in today has never been so high, not in many decades. This is not what we are aiming for. We need to do everything we can to live in a world in which relations between states are based on law, in which relations are predictable, in which the environment can be created and protected to ensure that everyone is answerable for their actions, especially in cases of violations of human rights. In conclusion, Vice-President, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, together we must get a grip on this situation that we are seeing today. Sometimes it's the case that nothing happens over decades, and then suddenly, all in one week, decades go by. This moment is now, and we must seize it to build a more just and safer world. And in a world that is constantly changing, we need to return to the fundamentals, that is, defense of human rights, defense of the rule of law, defense of democracy. We need to do this together.
